issues.subcategory: Frequentist terminology applied to Bayesian outputs
issues.description: The Results section labels Bayesian credible intervals as '95% Confidence Intervals,' which is a fundamental conceptual and terminological error. Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals have different definitions and interpretations. The Methods section correctly states '95% credible intervals were used to make inferences,' creating an internal inconsistency. Later in the same Results section the authors correctly use 'HPDI,' making the terminology inconsistent even within a single section. Readers unfamiliar with the distinction may misinterpret the strength and meaning of the inferences.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h ... Generation 95% CI: (-0.34, 0.25), mean = -0.04

issues.subcategory: Statistically significant interaction described as null
issues.description: The 95% Bayesian credible interval for the Generation × Treatment interaction on understanding score is (0.03, 0.81), which entirely excludes zero—indicating credible evidence of a positive effect. Yet the authors immediately conclude 'these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects... individual understanding.' This is self-contradictory: by the authors' own inferential standard (CIs not crossing zero), this interaction is a reliable effect. The selective dismissal of a significant interaction while retaining non-significant effects as confirmatory evidence represents inconsistent application of the same decision rule.
issues.quote: Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: MaxSpeed discrepancy between payoff formula and optimization calculation
issues.description: The payoff formula sets MaxSpeed = 160 m/h as the upper bound for incentive calculation. However, the text claims 'the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h,' which is used as the ceiling for the '71% optimization' calculation: (145.7 − 123.6) / (154 − 123.6) ≈ 72.7%. These two values are contradictory. If the true maximum is 154 m/h, the payoff formula over-rewards performance above 154 m/h relative to the incentive design intent. If 160 m/h is achievable, the optimization percentage is inflated and the 154 m/h figure is incorrect. Neither value is derived or justified in the text.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h... [1 - ((MaxSpeed – RecordedSpeed) / (MaxSpeed – MinSpeed))] x 3 + Bonus with MaxSpeed = 160

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent generation count in optimization claim
issues.description: In the same paragraph, the text first states 'After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h' then immediately claims 'an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.' The chain design contains 5 distinct participant generations (Gen 1 through Gen 5), connected by 4 transmission events. The paper's use of 'five generations' and 'four cultural generations' to describe the same endpoint is ambiguous and internally inconsistent, confusing the number of agents with the number of transmission events.
issues.quote: After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to 145.7 m/h (95% HPDI: (138.5, 152.4))... These results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: Absence of individual (non-chain) control condition
issues.description: The study lacks a condition in which individuals work alone for the same total number of trials as a full chain (i.e., 25 trials). Without this control, it is impossible to attribute the observed improvement across generations to cultural transmission rather than to the simple accumulation of individual exploration across more trials. A single individual given 25 trials might match or exceed the performance of a 5-person chain, which would undermine the cultural evolution interpretation. This is a critical confound for the study's central claim that improvements arise from multi-generational cultural transmission.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track... The cultural niche hypothesis predicts that the speed of the wheel will increase with generations

issues.subcategory: Assigning speed = 0 to non-descending wheels in linear model
issues.description: Non-descending wheels are coded as speed = 0 and included in a Gaussian linear model. This is statistically inappropriate because non-descending represents a qualitatively different outcome (categorical failure) rather than a quantitative low speed. Mixing these with normally-distributed speed values violates the distributional assumptions of linear regression, inflates variance, and creates a bimodal outcome structure. A censored, zero-inflated, or hurdle model would be more appropriate. The severity increases because the early generations likely have more failures, systematically biasing the estimated generation effect.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.subcategory: MCMC sampling failure in primary comparative analysis
issues.description: Analysis 3 is the primary analysis comparing wheel speed between treatments—the most important test in the paper. The authors acknowledge that 'the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low.' Poor mixing and low effective sample sizes indicate that the posterior distributions in this model are not reliably estimated. The robustness checks (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5) are post-hoc and involve modified models, constituting an undisclosed form of analytic flexibility. Conclusions based on a model with sampling pathologies should be treated with considerable caution, but no uncertainty about model reliability is conveyed in the main text.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3). The robustness of the model estimates was checked by running additional models (see below).

issues.subcategory: Incorrect or unstated chance level for 3-option understanding test
issues.description: The understanding test allows three responses: 'Wheel 1,' 'Wheel 2,' or 'No difference.' If 'No difference' is never the correct answer (as implied by the physical setup), random responding across all three options gives an expected score of 10/3 ≈ 3.33. The paper reports average scores around 4.47–4.60 and shows a 'horizontal line' for 'expected score for random guessers' in Figure 2B. If this line is placed at 5.0 (as implied by describing these scores as 'barely above chance'), it misrepresents the chance baseline by ~50%, making participants appear to perform close to random when they are actually performing well above a properly computed chance level. The correct chance level is never stated in the manuscript.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: 'Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2' or 'No difference'... Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.subcategory: Non-blind data collection with experimenter manipulating apparatus
issues.description: The experimenter was not blind to experimental condition during data collection. More critically, the experimenter physically positioned the weights on the wheel for each trial based on participant choices. This creates a direct pathway for unintentional experimenter influence on the primary outcome measure. Small differences in how precisely weights are positioned (e.g., due to differential care or attention across conditions) could systematically bias speed measurements. No inter-rater reliability or mechanical check for weight positioning consistency is reported.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments... Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly.

issues.subcategory: Absent sample size justification
issues.description: The paper provides no power analysis or principled justification for 14 chains per treatment. The sole justification offered is that these numbers exceed those of prior published studies, which is not a valid basis for claims about adequate statistical power. With only 14 independent chains per condition, the study may be severely underpowered to detect small-to-moderate effects of theory transmission. This is particularly concerning given the wide credible intervals reported for the treatment effects on speed (CI spanning from −10.76 to +18.13 m/h), which are consistent with practically meaningful effects in either direction.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications.

issues.subcategory: Character limit artificially constrains theory content
issues.description: Transmitted theories were restricted to 340 characters. This constraint could artificially prevent participants from formulating or transmitting multidimensional causal models that integrate both the moment of inertia and center-of-mass principles. One of the study's central conclusions is that 'participants do not spontaneously create multidimensional causal theories but instead mainly produce simplistic models.' However, this finding may be partly an artefact of the 340-character limit, which would structurally prevent transmission of full, two-principle theories. The study cannot distinguish between a cognitive limitation and an artificial constraint.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...'

issues.subcategory: Sex-segregated chains without rationale or analysis
issues.description: All chains were sex-segregated ('exclusively males or exclusively females'), but no justification for this design choice is provided. Sex differences in spatial reasoning, physics intuition, or social learning could systematically influence performance and understanding. The paper reports 70 women and 70 men total, presumably with 7 male and 7 female chains per treatment, yet sex is never included as a covariate or analyzed as a moderator. If sex differences exist, the sex-segregated design would confound chain identity with participant sex, potentially inflating between-chain variance.
issues.quote: participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc deviation from pre-registered analysis without full reporting
issues.description: The preregistered Analysis 4 modeled inertia and center-of-mass understanding scores separately with 'Physical Principle' and 'Physical Principle:Treatment' as predictors. This preregistered model was abandoned because it 'did not converge,' and the authors switched to an aggregated score analysis. The decision to aggregate loses important information—specifically, the differential effects of theory type on understanding of each physical principle, which is central to the paper's conclusions in Figure 3I. Model non-convergence is itself unreported: readers cannot evaluate what convergence criteria were used, whether alternative parameterizations were attempted, or whether the non-convergence reflects a genuine incompatibility between data and preregistered model structure.
issues.quote: the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable 'Physical Principle' in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: Unpreregistered exploratory analyses drive key conclusions
issues.description: The theory coding scheme, the categorization of theories into four types (inertia, center of mass, full, irrelevant), the heat-map analyses of exploration patterns, and the comparison of understanding scores by theory type (Figure 3) are described as 'exploratory analyses.' Yet these analyses support several of the paper's most novel and headline claims—that theory transmission constrains exploration and biases understanding. These analyses involve multiple researcher degrees of freedom: the four-category theory taxonomy, the grouping of 'Configurations' participants into 'balanced/unbalanced/various' categories, and the choice of which comparisons to highlight. No corrections for multiple comparisons are reported, and there is no discussion of how these categorization choices could have been made differently.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants' exploration behavior... participants' theories were coded according to whether they contained information related to moment of inertia, information related to the position of the wheel's centre of mass, both, or neither.

issues.subcategory: Understanding measure captures only explicit declarative knowledge
issues.description: The paper's measure of 'causal understanding' consists exclusively of explicit predictive judgments about paired wheel configurations. However, the authors themselves note that 'participants did not randomly explore the parameter space' and 'had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration'—demonstrating that participants possessed functional, implicit causal knowledge sufficient to guide productive behavior. These two observations are treated as independent rather than as evidence of a construct validity gap: the understanding test fails to capture implicit/procedural knowledge. Conclusions that 'causal understanding is not necessary' rest on a narrow operationalization of understanding that likely underestimates participants' actual causal competence.
issues.quote: participants did not randomly explore the parameter space... participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.subcategory: Theory-type effect on understanding may reflect individual differences rather than theory transmission
issues.description: The paper claims that inheriting a unidimensional theory causally constrains exploration and skews understanding. However, participants who wrote and transmitted a particular type of theory may have done so because of pre-existing cognitive tendencies or knowledge that also drove their exploration and understanding scores. Participants are not randomly assigned to receive a given theory type—they receive whatever the previous person in their chain wrote. Chains that tend to produce inertia-related theories may differ systematically from chains that produce center-of-mass theories in terms of prior knowledge, personality, or task approach. No within-person design or matching procedure controls for this confound.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass; symmetrically, inheriting a centre-of-mass-related theory increased their understanding of centre of mass, but decreased their understanding about inertia.

issues.subcategory: Cultural transmission effect conflated with practice-trial accumulation
issues.description: The core causal claim is that improvement arises from multi-generational cultural transmission. However, each chain accumulates up to 25 trials in total (5 per participant × 5 participants). Without an individual-alone condition with equivalent total trials, observed performance improvements could result from participants simply having access to configurations explored by previous individuals (equivalent to a richer starting point), or from a selection effect where better-performing configurations are retained—without any transmission of tacit knowledge. The design conflates informational transmission with trial accumulation.
issues.quote: our experiment shows that highly optimized technologies can emerge from the accumulation of many improvements made across generations linked by cultural transmission, without the need for an accurate causal understanding

issues.subcategory: Over-extrapolation from simple 2D task to complex real-world technologies
issues.description: The paper repeatedly draws inferences about the origins of technologies like bows and kayaks from a two-dimensional optimization task. The authors themselves acknowledge that the wheel task is 'low-dimensional' and describe it as 'a conservative test.' However, conclusions such as 'complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning' are drawn directly from this simple task. In a genuinely high-dimensional space, random improvements would become increasingly unlikely, and causal reasoning might be essential to navigate the fitness landscape efficiently. The leap from a 2D problem to 'complex' multi-hundred-dimensional technologies is theoretically unjustified and empirically untested.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD university student sample used to make claims about human cultural evolution
issues.description: All participants were university students recruited from universities in Lille, France—a WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) population. The paper draws broad inferences about human technology and cultural evolution. The authors briefly note this limitation and call for cross-cultural work, but the Discussion presents conclusions about 'humans' and 'human technology' without adequately qualifying them. Formal education in physics or engineering was controlled as a covariate, but general numeracy, familiarity with mechanical devices, and cultural priors about physical systems likely differ substantially across populations in ways that are not addressed.
issues.quote: Future cross-cultural work involving non WEIRD participants should tell us whether this selective exploration is culturally constructed or shared across populations... our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities

issues.subcategory: Failure rates not formally analyzed; 'No difference' response frequency unreported
issues.description: Non-descending wheel failures are visually depicted in Figure 2 as vertical bars but are never formally analyzed. Differential failure rates across generations or treatments could confound the speed analysis (since failures are coded as speed = 0). No statistics are provided for failure counts by generation, treatment, or their interaction. Additionally, the frequency with which participants chose 'No difference' in the understanding test is never reported. This response option is theoretically important: high use of 'No difference' could indicate uncertainty rather than understanding, and differential use across groups could bias score comparisons.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment... For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: 'Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2' or 'No difference'.

issues.subcategory: Title and conclusions overstate generality given operationalization constraints
issues.description: The paper's title states 'Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology,' a universal negative claim. This claim rests on: (a) one specific physical apparatus, (b) an explicit understanding measure that captures only verbal-declarative knowledge while participants demonstrably possessed implicit knowledge, (c) only 4 generational transitions, (d) a simple 2D optimization problem. The paper does not test whether causal understanding is necessary for more complex technological challenges. The title's use of 'not necessary' as a universal claim cannot be supported by a single paradigm that tests one type of understanding in one type of task over a short timescale.
issues.quote: Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology... our experiment shows that highly optimized technologies can emerge from the accumulation of many improvements made across generations linked by cultural transmission, without the need for an accurate causal understanding of the system.

issues.subcategory: Restriction to last two trials introduces selection bias
issues.description: Speed analyses are restricted to 'participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.' This creates a form of outcome-dependent sample restriction: participants who improve more rapidly within their session (and thus have fewer failures in later trials) are more fully represented. If improvement within a session is correlated with between-session improvement, this restriction inflates the observed generation effect. Moreover, the rationale—limiting failures—is addressed by already coding failures as speed = 0, making the restriction redundant and potentially introducing bias.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.
